problem: Source: "mists as chill as death wandered to the impulse of east winds along those purple peaks" — the east winds driving the mists are dropped.
new_text: I also discovered that a great pleasure—a joy bounded only by the horizon—lay beyond the high, spike-topped walls of our garden. This pleasure was the view: noble summits encircling a great green valley, and a bright stream full of dark stones and sparkling eddies. How different this scene had looked when I first saw it under the iron winter sky, frozen stiff, shrouded in snow! When mists as cold as death drifted on the east winds along those purple peaks and rolled down into the hollows until they merged with the frozen fog of the stream! That stream had been a torrent then, muddy and wild, tearing through the woods and sending a roaring sound through the air, often thickened with driving rain or whirling sleet. And the forest on its banks had shown only ranks of bare skeletons.

problem: Source: "on the banks of the A——" — the novel's redacted-name convention (kept elsewhere as "——shire" in the same paragraph) is flattened to "a river".
new_text: I studied the letter for a long time. The handwriting was old-fashioned and a bit shaky, like an elderly lady's. This was reassuring. A private fear had nagged me that in acting on my own, without guidance, I might get into some kind of trouble. Above all, I wanted the outcome to be respectable, proper, en règle. Now I felt that an elderly lady was a comforting element. Mrs. Fairfax! I pictured her in a black dress and widow's cap—cold, perhaps, but not uncivil. A model of elderly English respectability. Thornfield! That was obviously the name of her house. I imagined a neat, orderly place, though I couldn't form a clear picture of it. Millcote, ——shire—I refreshed my memory of the map of England. Yes, I found it. The county was seventy miles closer to London than the remote region where I lived now. That appealed to me. I longed to go somewhere with life and movement. Millcote was a large manufacturing town on the banks of the A———a busy place, no doubt. All the better. It would be a complete change, at least. Not that I was particularly attracted to the idea of factory chimneys and smoke—"but," I told myself, "Thornfield is probably a good distance from the town."
